summary.text: This paradox involves a coin-flipping game whose expected payoff is infinite, yet it seems to be worth only a small amount to players.
It shows that a decision rule using only expected value can recommend something that presumably no real person would do.
One classical resolution uses diminishing marginal utility of money: the same gain matters more to a pauper than to a rich man.

facts.label: Name origin
facts.value: Daniel Bernoulli's 1738 analysis in Saint Petersburg

facts.label: Expected win
facts.value: Grows without bound, so it is infinite

facts.label: Log-utility price
facts.value: A millionaire would pay up to $20.88

facts.label: Finite casino
facts.value: Expected value grows only logarithmically with its resources

items.prompt: A game has an infinite expected payoff, yet a stall at the fair charges $1,000 to enter and most people walk past. Why is that called a paradox?

options.label: Nobody can actually win the prize
Expected value says to pay any price, but people won't
The stall must be cheating its customers
People always overpay for games like this

items.explain: A criterion that counts only expected value says to play at any price, which clashes with what people are willing to pay.

items.prompt: Why might a gain of one thousand ducats mean more to a poor person than to a rich one, and how does that help with the paradox?

options.label: Money's use shrinks as wealth grows
Rich people never take gambles at all
Poor people can't count large sums well
Prices are set by how much cash is owned

items.explain: The classical resolution rests on diminishing marginal utility of money, so value depends on usefulness, not just the amount.

items.prompt: Using logarithmic utility, who should be willing to pay more to enter the game: a millionaire or someone with $1,000?

options.label: The person with $1,000, who has more to gain
Both the same, as the game is identical
The millionaire, whose wealth is much larger
Nobody, as the price is too high for all

items.explain: The willingness to pay depends on wealth: up to $20.88 for the millionaire versus $10.95 for the person with $1,000.

items.prompt: A casino has a limited bankroll. Even the largest one conceivable is used. What happens to the game's expected value?

options.label: It stays infinite regardless of the bankroll
It becomes negative for the casino's players
It doubles every time the bankroll doubles
It becomes quite modest

items.explain: Because it grows only logarithmically with the casino's resources, the expected value is quite modest even for a very large bankroll.

items.prompt: Why would ignoring very unlikely events make the game less tempting to a player?

options.label: Only rare events pay the huge prizes
Rare events always cost the player money
The casino refuses to pay rare wins
Ignoring them removes the coin flips

items.explain: People are conjectured to neglect unlikely events, and only unlikely events yield the high prizes behind the infinite expected value.

items.prompt: Someone says a square-root measure of satisfaction fully solves the paradox. Why is that not completely satisfying?

options.label: Square roots can't be applied to money at all
The paradox only appears for very rich players
Nobody has proposed square roots before now
The game can be changed to pay even faster and the paradox returns

items.explain: Changing the game so it gives even more rapidly increasing payoffs makes the paradox reappear.
